title: Posterior corner plot: what do the parameter posteriors look like?
summary: After inference, what do the parameters look like? A corner plot shows each parameter's marginal distribution on the diagonal and every pair's joint distribution below, so you see the width, the shape and the correlations of the posterior at once.

media.alt: A lower-triangular corner plot of three parameters: three teal histograms on the diagonal with vertical lines at the 16, 50 and 84 percent points and titles giving the median and uncertainties (for example 1.03 plus 0.21 minus 0.20); below the diagonal, grey scatter plots with teal 68 percent and blue 95 percent contour lines and an amber plus at the true value.
media.caption: Reference render of class F8.8 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: What do the parameter posteriors look like?
read_the_figure.axes: Diagonal: histogram of one parameter (theta1, theta2, theta3) with its own x axis and no y axis. Lower triangle: scatter of samples for each pair, with contours enclosing 68 and 95 percent of the posterior mass; axes are the parameter values.
look_at: How wide is each marginal, and does it look Gaussian, skewed or multimodal?
What is the tilt and thickness of each pair's contours (correlation)?
Is the true or reference value (the amber marker) inside the 68 percent region?
Are the credible levels and the percentile lines explained?
as_drawn: 3000 samples of three parameters. The diagonal titles give the median and the 16 and 84 percent offsets: theta1 1.03 (+0.21, -0.20), theta2 -0.54 (+0.29, -0.30), theta3 2.08 (+0.39, -0.41).

The contours enclose 68 percent (teal) and 95 percent (blue) of the density. The theta1-theta2 contours tilt up to the right (positive correlation about 0.33), theta1-theta3 slightly down (about -0.19), theta2-theta3 up (about 0.25).

Dashed amber lines and plus signs mark the true values (1.0, -0.5, 2.0), which the render states is synthetic; all lie well inside the 68 percent contours. The medians are offset from the truth by only 0.03, 0.04 and 0.08.
No chain diagnostics (convergence, effective sample size) are shown, and the prior is not drawn, so the plot cannot show how much the data taught.
read_the_figure.proves: The posterior samples show what parameter values are consistent with the data and the prior, and how they trade off. They do not show that the sampler converged, that the model is right, or that the posterior differs from the prior.
if_wrong: Banana-shaped or multimodal contours labelled with a single median and symmetric error: the summary hides the shape.
No reference values: the reader cannot tell whether the posterior is centred on the right place; with real data show the prior or a known value.
Samples from a chain that did not converge: the plot is a picture of the sampler, not the posterior.
must_check: marginals + pairwise: the marginals give the width of each parameter and the pairwise panels give the correlations that a list of intervals would hide.

terms.meaning: The probability distribution of the parameters given the data and the prior.
The distribution of one parameter with the others integrated out.
A region containing a stated share (68 or 95 percent) of the posterior mass.
The median with offsets to the 16th and 84th percentiles, about plus or minus one standard deviation for a Gaussian.
The tilt of a pair's contours; tells which parameter changes compensate each other.
A triangular grid of the marginals (diagonal) and the pairwise joint distributions.

remember: For a 2-D Gaussian the 68 percent contour is the ellipse at Mahalanobis squared distance 2.28 and the 95 percent at 5.99.
The 16 to 84 percentile offsets are about one sigma for a Gaussian.
A wide marginal means the parameter is poorly constrained.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: On the diagonal, bars give the histogram of one parameter's samples; solid white and dotted lines mark the median and the 16 and 84 percent points, and the title prints the numbers. Below the diagonal, grey dots are a thinned set of posterior samples for a pair and two contour lines enclose 68 percent (teal) and 95 percent (blue) of the density. Amber dashed lines and plus signs mark the true value.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Plain language: inference gives you not one best value but a cloud of plausible values. Each parameter's histogram shows how well it is pinned down; each pair's contour shows how they trade off, for example 'if theta1 is higher then theta2 must be higher too'. A corner plot puts all of these in one picture, which a table of intervals cannot, because intervals hide correlation.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Two-dimensional contours are projections of a higher-dimensional cloud and can hide structure in three or more parameters. Contours are drawn from a kernel density estimate whose bandwidth is a choice, and the 95 percent contour is the noisiest. Percentile titles with symmetric-looking errors hide skew or multiple modes. And a corner plot of samples says nothing about whether the sampler converged or the model is adequate.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A table of medians, intervals and the correlation matrix (F8.2) is the numerical version. Trace plots and the Gelman-Rubin statistic check the sampler. A posterior predictive band (F8.3) shows what the posterior implies for the data. For many parameters, plot only the pairs that matter.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Overlay the prior as a faint grey curve on each marginal, add the chain diagnostics (R-hat and effective sample size) as small text in each diagonal panel, and shade the 95 percent region instead of drawing only its boundary.

steps.title: The percentile summary and sigma
steps.note: For a Gaussian marginal the offsets are close to the standard deviation: here 0.20, 0.30 and 0.40 are the true values, and the render reads 0.20, 0.30 and 0.40 within rounding.

steps.note: Verified by simulation: 68.0 and 95.1 percent of samples fall inside these ellipses.

worked.title: Reading the posterior corner plot of the reference render
worked.problem: (1) Which parameter is best constrained (relative to its value)? (2) What do the tilts of the pair contours say? (3) Is the true value inside the 68 percent region in each panel?

solution.text: (1) Relative widths: sigma over the median.
Theta1 and theta3 are about equally well constrained in relative terms; theta2 is the worst.
(2) Theta1 and theta2 rise together (rho 0.33), theta2 and theta3 rise together (0.25) and theta1 and theta3 trade off weakly (-0.19). All are modest: the ellipses are close to circles.
(3) The amber plus lies well inside the teal 68 percent contour in all three panels; the medians are off the truth by only 0.03, 0.04 and 0.08, a fraction of the sigmas.

worked.answer: Theta1 and theta3 are constrained to about 19 percent, theta2 to 56 percent; correlations are +0.33, -0.19 and +0.25; the true value lies well inside the 68 percent contour in every panel (within 0.2 sigma).

analyze.q: Why does a 2-D contour of a 3-parameter posterior not capture everything?
A marginal has two humps. What is wrong with a title giving a single median and symmetric errors?
How would you verify that the samples come from a converged chain?
analyze.hint: Several chains, R-hat, effective sample size.

evaluate.q: The true value lies inside the 68 percent region in all panels. What does that show and what does it not?

create: Overlay the prior on each marginal and add R-hat to each diagonal panel.
Repeat with 100 synthetic data sets and plot where the truth falls in each posterior (a calibration histogram).

checks.q: What does the tilt of a contour tell you?
checks.answer: How the two parameters are related in the posterior: an upward tilt means that they increase together, so the data constrain a combination better than each alone.

checks.q: A marginal reads 2.0 (+0.3, -0.3). What is its standard deviation approximately, and what interval holds about 95 percent?
checks.hint: 16 to 84 is about plus or minus one sigma.
checks.answer: Sigma is about 0.3, so the 95 percent interval is about 2.0 plus or minus 0.6 (1.4 to 2.6).

checks.q: Two parameters have contours that form a long thin diagonal ridge. What does it mean for their individual intervals?
checks.answer: Each parameter alone is poorly constrained, but a combination is well constrained: the intervals are wide while the joint region is thin; report the combination or reparametrise.
